content.title: About
content.content: Vegetables are edible parts of plants—roots, leaves, stems, and fruits—commonly used as base and flavoring agents in soups. They add taste, aroma, color, and nutrients to the dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vegetable soups have been made since antiquity; the Romans prepared a thick vegetable broth called "potage".
Different vegetables need different cooking times: root vegetables (carrot, beet) take longer, while leafy greens (spinach, parsley) are added at the end.
Vegetable soups are often low‑calorie and high in fiber, making them popular in weight‑loss diets.
There are over 100 types of soups where vegetables are the main ingredient, from French "vichyssoise" to Japanese miso.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: Vegetables provide vitamins A, C, K and B‑complex, which support immunity, vision and metabolism.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: They contain potassium, magnesium, iron and calcium, essential for heart function and bone health.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber improves digestion, promotes satiety and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Vegetable soups typically contain little saturated fat, benefiting cardiovascular health.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytonutrients such as carotenoids and polyphenols protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy to specific vegetables
items.content: Some individuals may react to tomatoes, peppers or celery.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Improperly washed vegetables can retain pesticide residues.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Vegetables like spinach and beet are high in oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stones in susceptible people.

items.title: Nutrient loss with prolonged boiling
items.content: Extended cooking can reduce vitamin C and some B‑vitamin levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add vegetables to soups diced, grated, or pureed. They can be simmered in broth, roasted before adding, or tossed in as fresh greens at the end for aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh vegetables in the refrigerator’s crisper drawer, loosely packed in perforated bags. Cooked vegetable soups should be cooled quickly and stored in airtight containers in the fridge for up to 3‑4 days.
